rounds.text: Kalyani Steels Ltd trades at an attractive P/E of 13.1x against a sector benchmark of 21.44x, alongside an EV/EBITDA of 7.66x compared to its sector benchmark of 12.02x [E1, E6, E11]. The business demonstrates solid fundamental returns, delivering an ROA of 9.02% and an ROCE of 13.91%, both beating sector benchmarks [E8, E10]. Valuation disconnect is highlighted by a discounted cash flow model indicating an intrinsic value of Rs 1183 per share against a market price of Rs 865, offering a margin of safety of 26.9% [E41, E42]. Operational momentum is supported by an operating margin expansion to 22% in September 2026 from 19% in the year-ago quarter, alongside a healthy free cash flow of Rs 80 Cr in March 2026 [E27, E32]. Conceded: cash conversion stands at 0.55x for March 2026 with profits far ahead of cash [E30].

Despite the optical cheapness implied by headline multiples, Kalyani Steels carries significant hidden risks in its earnings quality and financial stability [E30, E56]. Cash conversion is poor at 0.55x for March 2026, indicating that reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash generation and pointing toward potential issues with receivables or accruals [E30]. Furthermore, the company is flagged as potentially capitalizing its interest cost, which casts doubt on the true sustainability of its reported earnings [E56]. Compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months has contracted by -1%, demonstrating top-line stagnation even as longer-term historical growth remains modest at 5% over 10 years [E14, E16]. Balance sheet pressures are also mounting, with total borrowings rising to Rs 530 Cr in September 2026 compared to Rs 475 Cr a year earlier [E35]. Institutional confidence is faltering, evidenced by foreign institutions reducing their holdings to 1.91% from 2.71% and overall institutional money flow registering negative [E38, E40]. Finally, the stock suffers from extreme historical volatility of 68.6% and a catastrophic worst peak-to-trough drawdown of -77.1%, underlining severe structural downside risks for investors [E49, E50]. Conceded: [E1]

While the bear highlights a cash conversion ratio of 0.55x [E30], this figure must be weighed against the company’s actual generation of Rs 141 Cr in operating cash flow and Rs 80 Cr in free cash flow during the same period [E31, E32]. The concern regarding interest capitalization [E56] is mitigated by the company’s conservative debt-to-equity ratio of 0.24x and a comfortable current ratio of 2.14x, which demonstrate strong financial health [E33, E34]. Although the bear points to a 1% contraction in trailing twelve-month sales [E16], this is countered by a 10% growth in profit over the same period and a significant 3 percentage point increase in quarterly operating margins [E19, E27]. Regarding institutional outflows [E38, E40], these are offset by the fact that domestic institutions have increased their stake by 1.28 percentage points since December 2023 [E39]. Conceded: [E49, E50]. The stock’s valuation remains highly attractive, with a P/E of 13.01x and EV/EBITDA of 7.66x, both of which sit well below their respective sector benchmarks of 21.44x and 12.02x [E6, E11].

The bull points to Rs 141 Cr in operating cash flow and Rs 80 Cr in free cash flow [E31, E32], but overlooks that a 0.55x cash conversion means reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash collections due to potential receivables or accruals issues [E30]. While the bull cites a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of 0.24x and a current ratio of 2.14x to dismiss interest capitalization concerns [E33, E34, E56], borrowings have actually climbed to Rs 530 Cr in September 2026 from Rs 475 Cr a year prior [E35]. The bull counters a 1% trailing sales contraction with profit growth and margin expansion [E16, E19, E27], but ignores that yearly and quarterly operating-margin trends are both explicitly flagged as inconsistent [E28, E29]. Conceded: [E39].
